title: WNBA Prop Picks: First Basket, Team to Score First & More
text:
Home›WNBA Picks
Slam Dunk Bets projects first-event props for every WNBA game, regular season and playoffs, with the same models we use for the NBA. Projections are compared to the prices at eight sportsbooks every 30 minutes, and the edges post to Discord with recommended unit sizes. Every recommended bet is graded and published. Across three WNBA seasons the record is +1,390 net units on 13,668 wagers, a 16.0% return on units staked.

title: WNBA Prop Picks: First Basket, Team to Score First & More
text:
How the picks work
The models are the same ones that produce our NBA picks, trained on WNBA play-by-play data: who wins the tipoff, which team scores first, which player scores first for their team, and how. A play is alerted when a book’s price is at least 1.5 percentage points better than our projected probability, with Kelly-based unit sizes scaled so the average play is about one unit. How Do You Predict First Baskets? covers the pipeline.
WNBA slates are smaller than NBA slates, two to six games on most days, and books post fewer markets per game. In 2026 we alerted about 33 plays per game day. Starting lineups are usually confirmed close to tipoff, and that is when the largest edges appear.

title: WNBA Prop Picks: First Basket, Team to Score First & More
text:
What an alert looks like
Alerts post to Discord grouped by game, sorted from largest edge to smallest, with every qualifying book, its price and the recommended units on each line. 🚨 marks a new play, 🚀 a new daily-best price, ⬇️ a play that is off its peak. The same plays, with every book’s price and line movement, are in the Slam Dunk Dashboard.

Which sportsbooks do the WNBA picks cover?
FanDuel, DraftKings, Fanatics, BetMGM, theScore, BetRivers, Hard Rock and Caesars. FanDuel and DraftKings carried about 86% of our 2026 volume. Each alert lists every book where the play qualifies.


Do WNBA picks run all season?
Yes: from opening night through the Finals, including the Commissioner’s Cup. There are no picks on days with no games, and WNBA picks and NBA picks run at the same time when the seasons overlap in May and June.


Is one subscription for both the NBA and the WNBA?
Yes. One subscription covers every league we project: NBA, WNBA, MLB, NFL and NHL.

Plans start at $19.99 a week with a 30-day free trial; details on the Subscribe page. You must be 21 or older. Past results do not guarantee future results.

title: Stats: Who Scores First, Who Keeps the First Inning Clean
text:
Home›Stats
These pages answer the questions bettors ask before a first basket or first-inning bet: who scores first for this team, how often does the home team score first, which starters keep the first inning clean. Everything is counted from the play-by-play and the official line scores, not from a sportsbook, and rebuilt from the data as seasons progress.
The stats are history. The picks come from models that combine this history with tonight’s lineups, the opponent, the park, the weather and the price at every book.

title: Stats: Who Scores First, Who Keeps the First Inning Clean
text:
NBA
NBA first basket stats: the players with the most first baskets, the highest rate per start, how often each team scores first and wins the tipoff, and how first baskets are scored. Then one page per team with who scores first for them, home and away, by phase of the season, with the jump-ball record and the previous season for comparison.
Atlanta Hawks · Boston Celtics · Brooklyn Nets · Charlotte Hornets · Chicago Bulls · Cleveland Cavaliers · Dallas Mavericks · Denver Nuggets · Detroit Pistons · Golden State Warriors · Houston Rockets · Indiana Pacers · LA Clippers · Los Angeles Lakers · Memphis Grizzlies · Miami Heat · Milwaukee Bucks · Minnesota Timberwolves · New Orleans Pelicans · New York Knicks · Oklahoma City Thunder · Orlando Magic · Philadelphia 76ers · Phoenix Suns · Portland Trail Blazers · Sacramento Kings · San Antonio Spurs · Toronto Raptors · Utah Jazz · Washington Wizards: all linked from the NBA leaders page.

title: Stats: Who Scores First, Who Keeps the First Inning Clean
text:
WNBA
WNBA first basket stats: the same tables for the WNBA season, with a page for each of the 15 teams.

title: Stats: Who Scores First, Who Keeps the First Inning Clean
text:
MLB
MLB NRFI stats: how often there is no run in the first inning, by team, at home and away, by month, and for every starting pitcher with 15 or more starts. Then one page per team with their NRFI record, how often they score and allow a first-inning run, and every starter’s first-inning record.

title: Stats: Who Scores First, Who Keeps the First Inning Clean
text:
How to use these numbers
A high rate is not a bet. Books price first baskets from the same starting lineups and first-inning markets from the same starters, so a player who scores first in 30% of starts is only worth a bet when a book offers better than 30%, after tonight’s lineup and opponent are accounted for. The guides explain how each market works, and the market pages show what our models have returned on each one.

Where do these stats come from?
NBA and WNBA first baskets, first points and tipoffs are labeled from the official play-by-play and box scores. MLB first-inning runs come from the official inning-by-inning line scores, and starting pitchers from the posted probables. Pages note the date they were last rebuilt.


How often are the stats updated?
They are rebuilt from the data periodically during each season, and always after a season ends. The current season appears once enough games have been played to mean something.


Are these the picks?
No. The picks post to Discord for subscribers, from models that use this history plus the day’s lineups, prices and conditions. These pages are the public context behind them.

text:
How we counted

Wagers and plays. A play is one recommendation: a player or team, in one market, in one game. When a price improves after the first alert, we recommend adding to the play, and each addition is logged as a separate wager. The same play at a different sportsbook is also a separate wager.
Units. Wager sizes are standardized so that the average recommended wager is about one unit. Net units are winnings minus losses. ROI is net units divided by units staked.
Voided wagers. 427 wagers were voided by the sportsbook, for example when a player did not play. They are excluded from every figure above.
Completeness. The figures include every other wager we alerted through October 4, at the price posted when we alerted it. Prediction exchanges are not included.
Sportsbooks. FanDuel accounted for 45% of units staked, at an 11.8% ROI. DraftKings accounted for 41%, at a 1.0% ROI. The rest was spread across Fanatics, BetMGM, theScore, BetRivers, Hard Rock and Caesars.

title: How Do We Predict Home Runs? Part 4: Alert Alert, Home Run Edition
text: If you read our first-baskets series, you already know we’re obsessive about the last mile. A projection that never reaches you, or reaches you stale, might as well not exist. So the whole system runs like a tiny newspaper with an extremely niche beat.

title: How Do We Predict Home Runs? Part 4: Alert Alert, Home Run Edition
text:
The daily schedule
Every Monday at 2am, the models retrain on everything through the day before. Every morning at 6am, a full refresh: schedules, rosters, park factors, yesterday’s plays graded and logged. And then every 30 minutes from 7am to 10pm ET, a tick: pull the newest pitch data, check for posted lineups and probable starters, grab a fresh hourly forecast for every ballpark, re-simulate every game whose inputs actually changed (the fingerprint trick from Part 2), re-price 13 books, and push alerts.

title: How Do We Predict Home Runs? Part 4: Alert Alert, Home Run Edition
text:
Weather, resolved per ballpark
Weather gets the full nerd treatment, by the way. Wind “blowing out” isn’t a vibe — every forecast is resolved against the actual compass bearing from home plate to center field in that specific park, so a gust that’s blowing out in one stadium is a crosswind in another. Domes are a permanent 72°F and windless, which is boring, but boring is easy to model. Retractable roofs get a per-game open-or-closed call.

title: How Do We Predict Home Runs? Part 4: Alert Alert, Home Run Edition
section: What a home run alert looks like
text:
What a home run alert looks like
Alerts land in Discord looking like this:

LAA @ TEX (8:05 pm ET)

Josh Lowe 1+ (proj +519): +750 br (2.5u), +720 dk (2.3u), …
Jorge Soler 2+ (proj +545): +600 br (0.7u)


Games in start-time order, plays sorted by edge, every qualifying book listed with its price and recommended units, best value first. And the emoji do actual work:

🚨 first time a play qualifies today
🚀 new day-high in value — the market moved further from us
⬇️ still playable, but off its peak
📖 a new book just joined the party

The high-water marks reset at midnight ET, so a 🚀 is always a genuinely new best — a play that faded and crawled back to a price it already hit today gets a ⬇️, never a fresh rocket.

title: How Do We Predict Home Runs? Part 4: Alert Alert, Home Run Edition
text:
Projections freeze at first pitch
And when a game goes live, we stop. Projections freeze at first pitch — no in-game re-pricing, no chasing. Pregame edges are our lane, and we stay in it.

title: How Do We Predict Home Runs? Part 4: Alert Alert, Home Run Edition
text:
The Slam Dunk Dashboard
If Discord isn’t your speed, the same numbers live in the Slam Dunk Dashboard at app.slamdunk.bet: one card per game, with the weather, projected lineups, first-inning odds, and per-batter home run odds. And because we archive the full edge table on every single odds refresh, the app can show you how prices moved through the day — when the books adjusted, which direction, and whether the value is growing or already got eaten.
And that’s the machine: 119 columns on every pitch, six million pitches of training data, a chain of models, an exact little 72-cell plate-appearance solve, 20,000 simulations per game, a calibration layer, 13 books twice an hour, half-Kelly sizing, and a rocket emoji when it matters. From data to dingers, we’ve covered the bases. For real this time — it’s baseball. The bases are literal.
Thanks as always for reading, holler if you have questions (@jimtheflash is the best way to find us), and if you want these alerts in your pocket, please consider subscribing — first month’s free — or come hang out in the Discord 🙏

How Do We Predict Home Runs? Part 1: Pitch Data · Part 2: Game-State Data · Part 3: From Projections to Edges · Part 4: Alert Alert, Home Run Edition

title: How Do We Predict Home Runs? Part 2: Game-State Data
section: Game state changes on every pitch
text:
Game state changes on every pitch
Everything in Part 1 is stuff we know before first pitch, and you could stop there: throw the pregame features into a model and get a decent baseline probability that a player goes deep. But pitches don’t happen in a vacuum, they happen inside games. Pitchers change their approach when they’re protecting a big lead or chasing from behind, when they’re ahead or behind in the count, when there are runners in scoring position. Batters do the same! With two strikes, the pitch mix tilts hard toward breaking and offspeed stuff — and as we covered in Part 1, breaking balls become dingers a lot less often than heaters do. Our models see all of it: balls, strikes, outs, all 24 combinations of runners and outs, the inning, the score difference, times through the order, home/away, and the handedness matchup.

title: How Do We Predict Home Runs? Part 2: Game-State Data
text:
Lineups, substitutions and plate appearances
And then there’s the obvious one: a player’s chances of homering in a game rise and fall with his plate appearances. So how a team moves through its lineup — and how it handles substitutions, for defense or pinch-hitting or pinch-running — matters a LOT. By the time the lineup turns over a third time, the 9-hole hitter is about three times as likely as the leadoff man to have been lifted, and some clubs go to their bench much faster than others. Our sim tracks per-slot survival odds and per-team pinch-hit tendencies for exactly this reason.
Given all that, it should be pretty clear: the state of the game is a real predictor of whether an at-bat produces a homer, and the state changes on every pitch. So how do you account for game states before the game even starts? SIMULATIONS.

title: How Do We Predict Home Runs? Part 2: Game-State Data
text:
Solving every plate appearance exactly
But first, a confession: we don’t actually roll dice pitch by pitch. For every batter-pitcher matchup, in every context, we solve the plate appearance EXACTLY. There are only 12 possible counts and six pitch classes, so a plate appearance is really a little 72-cell grid: push probability through every path — every pitch choice, every swing and take, every foul — until all of it has been absorbed into an outcome. Foul balls with two strikes just loop the count back on itself, and the math is perfectly happy to price the at-bat that takes a dozen foul balls to resolve. Out the other side comes an exact distribution for that matchup: strikeout, walk, hit-by-pitch, single, double, triple, homer, out. No randomness, no simulation noise, just probability doing its job.

title: How Do We Predict Home Runs? Part 2: Game-State Data
text:
Then 20,000 simulations per game
THEN we roll dice. We simulate each game 20,000 times, plate appearance by plate appearance, through a full game-state machine: lineups turning over, starters running out of gas, bullpens, pinch hitters, baserunners doing baserunner things (the sim knows a runner on second scores on a single about 60% of the time). The endings are score-aware, too: a home team that’s leading skips the bottom of the ninth, walk-offs end innings mid-stream, and ties go to extras with the free runner on second (yes, the Manfred runner lives in our simulator; no, he cannot be traded). Getting the endings right isn’t just cosmetic — it fixed a systematic ~5% inflation in home hitters’ projections, since home teams bat in the ninth a lot less often than a lazy sim assumes.
After 20,000 sims we can answer questions like, “in what percentage of sims for the Phillies-Dodgers game did Ohtani go yard?” That proportion is our probability — the number that eventually becomes a projection, an edge, and maybe an alert. Why 20,000? Because at a 10% homer probability, that’s enough sims to shrink the random noise to about ±0.2 points — and in our testing, extra sims sharpen the PRICES, not the model. Backtest accuracy is flat whether we run 2,000 or 20,000. Precision is for the odds; accuracy was decided back in Part 1. (Also: everything is seeded, so every run is perfectly reproducible. The seed is 2026. Because of course it is.)

title: How Do We Predict Home Runs? Part 2: Game-State Data
text:
Keeping it fast
Now, simulating every game 20,000 times, then re-simulating all day as lineups post and weather shifts, sounds computationally expensive. Three tricks keep it manageable:

Solve once, sample cheap. The expensive part is the exact plate-appearance math — about three seconds of thinking per game. After that, each additional simulated game costs six hundredths of a millisecond.
Simulate wide. Instead of looping through 20,000 games one at a time, we advance all 20,000 together, one plate appearance per step, as big numpy arrays. The slow part of the code scales with the length of a game, not the number of sims.
Fingerprints. Every game’s projection carries a signature of its inputs: lineups, starters, weather (bucketed into 3°F and 2 mph steps, so ordinary forecast wobble doesn’t count as news). New update, same signature? Skip the re-run. And once a game goes live, its pregame projection freezes for good.

Add it up and a full slate re-scores in about the time it takes to microwave a burrito, on an old i7 with 16GB of RAM. Still just a couple of guys on laptops over here. V nifty.

title: How Do We Predict Home Runs? Part 2: Game-State Data
section: Calibration: when we say 12%, we mean 12%
text:
Calibration: when we say 12%, we mean 12%
One last step before the numbers are ready for prime time: calibration. An assembled simulator carries small compounding biases — ours ran a touch hot on balls in play, and its generic bullpens were a touch friendlier to hitters than real ones — so a final calibration layer, fit on held-out data, trues everything up. It stretches the tiniest probabilities upward (a raw 2% becomes about 4%) and trims the biggest ones (a raw 20% becomes about 17%). The goal is simple: when we publish 12%, we mean 12%.
So now we’ve got a calibrated probability that any batter in baseball goes deep tonight. A probability is not a bet, though. In Part 3 we turn projections into edges. Thanks for reading!

title: Why First Baskets?
text: Hello, thanks for visiting - and if you’re a subscriber, thanks even more!

title: Why First Baskets?
section: It started with legal betting in Illinois
text:
It started with legal betting in Illinois
Slam Dunk Bets started predicting first baskets in 2020, mostly because sports betting was just becoming legal in Illinois, and one of the sports books was running consistent specials on the market.
We discovered that most of the available books were offering first basket props, and that the odds usually varied from book to book.

title: Why First Baskets?
section: The data made the market modelable
text:
The data made the market modelable
The play-by-play data for NBA games was freely available, and could be parsed effectively using data science tools. This enabled us to develop models using machine learning tools to predict the likelihood of players to score first in a game.
Once we refined our models, we learned that first baskets were relatively predictable. “Relatively” is doing a lot of work in that sentence, of course, but by nerdy machine learning model evaluation metrics, we felt pretty good.

title: Why First Baskets?
section: Popular players are overpriced, and the inverse is true too
text:
Popular players are overpriced, and the inverse is true too
In addition, we learned that popular players were typically overpriced compared to what our models expected, which we think makes sense: popular players typically get more action from bettors, so books can get away with setting their opening prices high.
The inverse was also true - less popular players were often very favorably priced compared to what our models expected, i.e. they were often positive expected value (+EV). And that’s what we wanted to find!

title: Why First Baskets?
text:
So, why first baskets?
So to answer the question we raised rhetorically, we started out focusing on first basket markets because: the data were available to build models; the models we built were useful at predicting the thing we wanted to predict; our model predictions enabled us to find +EV bets to make.
Want to see how the models actually work? Start with Part 1 of the series, or check the FAQ for the markets we cover and the track record.

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 5: Alert Alert
text: I think this is gonna be the last part of the “How Do You Predict First Baskets?” series of posts! Woohoo, we made it! The last post is on the alerts themselves - how do we make the edges we identify actionable for our users?

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 5: Alert Alert
text:
Why every 30 minutes
We run our modeling pipeline every 30 minutes, where we both update our predictions, and update the odds from the sportsbooks. Why 30 minutes? Primarily to avoid pissing off the books and triggering security measures that could break our tools for getting the odds; 30 minutes seemed to capture the important movements that happen within the day; and 30 minute intervals captured the majority of the different tipoff times of NBA games.

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 5: Alert Alert
text:
What an alert contains
So every 30 minutes we have a batch of edges, and we send those to our Discord server, broken down by game, sorted by player from biggest edge to smallest, and sorted within player by books the biggest edge to smallest (we only show the edges for players, nothing that isn’t positive expected value).
The alerts also factor in what we’ve alerted on already: some players we’ve alrady alerted on earlier in the day, some players we’ve already alerted on but the edges are bigger or smaller than before, and some players are brand new.

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 5: Alert Alert
text:
What the emoji flags mean
We indicate brand new players in a prop market (or teams for team-level props) with a 🚨 emoji, since these bets always require action from our users, i.e. placing new bets. Similarly, when a player we’ve already alerted on in the day has a new best edge for that day, we add a 🚀 to their entry; these are also cases where our users will likely want to take action and add more to their original bets.
When a player’s best edge is no longer at it’s daily peak, we add a ⬇️ to the alert. This doesn’t require action by the user, unless they missed the previous alerts or didn’t place a wager then. But we include this information so that users can get an idea of how lines are moving around and when they might peak for different props or players.

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 5: Alert Alert
text:
When are lines softest?
An engaged reader might ask, “are there peak times when lines are at their softest?” Great question! The answer is “Yep”, and we tackled it in a followup: Is There A Best Time Of Day To Bet First Baskets?
We’re always trying to incrementally improve our alerts, by getting the odds faster (maybe someday the books will actually sell access to their odds APIs! nah jk they’re cowards), and calculating predictions in advance when we can.
And there it is. From data to alerts, we’ve covered the bases. Er, baskets. We’ve covered the baskets. Thanks for reading, and if you haven’t, please subscribe!

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 3: So Many Models
text: In the previous post on predicting first baskets, we walked through the data we use for the models. Next we’ll talk through the models themselves. This will get kinda long and nerdy!

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 3: So Many Models
text:
Ensembles, reduced models and reconciliation
We build a LOT of models. For each modeling problem, we typically build three unique kinds of models (e.g. regression, decision trees, splines) and combine them via a technique called ensembling. Ensemble models build off the idea of the wisdom of the crowds, a phenomena where often times the average estimate of something, like the weight of a cow, from a big crowd of people, is a better predictor of that thing than the estimates of experts. In ensemble models, we replace the crowd of people with a bunch of predictions from models, and try to do some smart weighting of the different input models as we get evidence about which models are most reliable.
But there’s more! Sometimes, the inputs to a model aren’t always available for every player or team - for instance, we can’t use any statistics that reference a previous season for rookies, or a 20-game average of a metric for a player or team who hasn’t played 20 games. So we build sets of models, called reduced models, to handle these different cases, and then use a process called reconciliation to align the outputs, which is important in cases where we’re using different models for different players in the same games.
Supporting all these models present a challenge for orchestration, i.e. figuring out which models to use in different situations, but has so far given us far stronger results than other approaches to the problem of predictors not always being available for every case that needs a prediction (like imputation).
So, to the models! Here’s that diagram again:

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 3: So Many Models
text:
Jump ball models
The first are the jump ball models, which predict the likelihood of a specific jumper to win the tip against another specific jumper, e.g. Anthony Davis to win the tip against Bam Adebayo or vice versa. A player’s win rate against a specific opponent is almost always the best predictor of the outcome here, but a number of other factors, like a player’s height, reach, vertical, and overall jump ball win rate are also useful pieces of information.

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 3: So Many Models
text:
Team to score first
Once we’ve predicted the tipoff winner, we can predict which team will score first. These models use the output of the jump ball models, along with game lines and other team-level stats like offensive efficiency (adjusted for the expected lineup). One note, is that defensive factors rarely explain much variance in first team to score outcomes - there might be some lockdown defensive teams out there, but the majority of the time a team’s offensive production is most important. These are also the only models in our stack that use odds data from the books, because frankly the models are a lot better performing when we include them; in the future we’d prefer to remove the dependency on external odds estimates, but for now they work.

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 3: So Many Models
section: Player to score first for their team
text:
Player to score first for their team
Independent from the jump ball and first team to score processes, we also model which player will score first for their team. This doesn’t require any knowledge of who will win the tipoff or which team scores first (we tested that). The most important features in our first team scorer models are focused on usage: players who have a lot of offensive touches early in the game tend to be more likely to score first, but this depends a great deal on who else is in the starting lineup that day and their expected usage.
This makes intuitive sense! For instance, if a player is typically a backup Center, they almost certainly have a low likelihood to score first in any given game; but if the starting Center is inactive and the backup moves into the starting lineup, the backup’s usage pattern has to be higher than what you’d expect in a “typical” game. Our data support that hypothesis and our models utilize it to a great advantage. (To be fair, the sportsbooks do this with their models too! We just do it better.)

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 3: So Many Models
section: Player to score first in the game
text:
Player to score first in the game
At this point we have all the main ingredients for our player to score the first basket for the game models. The most important inputs for these models are, unsurprisingly, the output of the team to score first models and the output of the player to score first for their team models. Most of the other information about player and team performance is already baked into the previous modeling steps!

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 3: So Many Models
text:
Exact-method models
The last pieces to the modeling puzzle are the exact methods for first team to score, first team player, and first player overall, e.g. predicting which player or team will score first and also specifying that it will happen on a two pointer or a free throw or a dunk (different books have different methods available). The most important features of these models are their predecessor models, and shot type trends adjusted for different lineup combinations.
And there it is! We might do some more technical writeups on modeling tools and techniques later down the line, as well as some pieces about how we predict other first events in basketball games (like rebounds or steals). But the next post, Part 4, is about how we find and quantify our edges to make play recommendations.
Thanks for reading all this, and if you haven’t yet, please subscribe to get the picks in our Discord server!

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 1: High Level Overview
text: Our first post outlined why we bet on first baskets, but doesn’t say anything at all about how we do it. These next posts will give some more context on our approach for predicting first basket outcomes. This first post will be a super high-level run through the process. Heck, I can even make a little diagram!

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 1: High Level Overview
text:
The pipeline in one diagram

I’ll walk through the boxes and arrows.

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 1: High Level Overview
text:
Step 1: Label the play-by-play data
First, we get a bunch of data from different sources, most importantly play-by-play records from the NBA and WNBA.
We use those data to flag the winning player for every jump ball, and who they beat, as well as which players and teams score first and how it happened.

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 1: High Level Overview
section: Step 2: Model the tipoff and the team to score first
text:
Step 2: Model the tipoff and the team to score first
Once the data are labeled, we build models to predict the winner of a jump ball between players A and B. These models enable us to predict which team is going to possess the ball first, and knowing which team will possess the ball first is hugely predictive of which team will score first.

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 1: High Level Overview
section: Step 3: Model the first scorer for each team
text:
Step 3: Model the first scorer for each team
We could stop here, because “player to win the tipoff” and “team to score first” are popular prop markets in their own rights, but we keep going! Independent of first possession, we can also model which player will score first for their team given a specific lineup; this is also a very popular (and profitable) prop market. Even more, we model out the odds of a player scoring first for their team with a specific method, like a free throw or a three pointer.

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 1: High Level Overview
section: Step 4: Combine them into first-basket odds
text:
Step 4: Combine them into first-basket odds
Finally, we can use the outputs of the team to score first and player to score first for their team models, to estimate the odds of a player scoring first for the entire game (and the method they use). Tada!
Now that you’ve got the high level view, we can start looking more specifically at different parts of the process. We can start with the data, in Part 2!

Home›NBA Picks›NBA Team to Score First & Win Tipoff Picks
Team to score first and win tipoff are the simplest first-event props: two outcomes, prices near even money. They are also the first two steps in our first-basket pipeline, so we project them for every NBA game. These are our thinnest-margin markets, and we say so. Over the last three seasons they returned +248 net units on 6,216 wagers, a 4.6% return on units staked.

title: NBA Team to Score First & Win Tipoff Picks
text:
The markets

Win tipoff: which player wins the opening jump ball. Usually priced between -130 and +130.
Team to score first: which team scores the game’s first points.
Team to score first exact method: the team and how it scores, for example a two-pointer. Longer prices, more ways to lose.

title: NBA Team to Score First & Win Tipoff Picks
text:
How we project them
The tipoff model predicts the chance that one specific jumper beats another. A player’s record against that specific opponent is the strongest input, with height, reach, vertical and overall jump-ball win rate behind it. The team-to-score-first model takes the tipoff projection and adds team-level inputs such as lineup-adjusted offensive efficiency and the game line. Defense matters surprisingly little here. These are the only models in our stack that use sportsbook odds as an input, because they perform better with them. Part 3 of the series has the details.

title: NBA First Basket Picks
text:
Home›NBA Picks›NBA First Basket Picks
First basket props were the first market we modeled, in 2020, and they are still our largest. Our models project the first scorer for every NBA game and every scoring method, compare those projections to the prices at nine sportsbooks every 30 minutes, and post the edges to Discord. Over the last three seasons, 37,374 tracked first-basket wagers returned +3,546 net units, a 12.9% return on units staked.

title: NBA First Basket Picks
section: What a first basket bet is
text:
What a first basket bet is
A first basket bet is a wager on which player scores the first points of the game. Books offer several versions of it:

First basket (also called first field goal or first points): the first player to score. Some books count free throws, some do not. Our alerts say which.
First basket exact method: the first scorer and how they score, for example a three-pointer or a dunk. Longer prices, bigger payouts.
First basket by team: the first player to score for one team, regardless of who scores first in the game. Two winners per game, so shorter prices.
First basket by team exact method: the team version with the scoring method added.
First basket type: how the game’s first points are scored, regardless of player.

title: NBA First Basket Picks
section: Why first baskets can be beaten
text:
Why first baskets can be beaten
Books price first-basket props inconsistently, and the prices move a lot during the day. Popular players tend to be overpriced because they draw the most betting action. Less popular players, including role players who move into a starting lineup when someone sits, are often underpriced relative to how often they take the first shot. Our models are built around exactly that: a player’s expected early usage in that night’s specific lineup. The full story is in Why First Baskets?

title: NBA First Basket Picks
text:
How we project first baskets
We label every jump ball and first basket in the NBA’s play-by-play data, then build models for each step: who wins the tipoff, which team scores first, which player scores first for their team, and how. Combining them gives a probability for every player and method in the game. The models are ensembles, retrained as the season goes, and reduced versions fill in when a player has too little history, such as a rookie. The five-part series starts with a high-level overview and ends with how the alerts work.
A play is alerted when a book’s price is at least 1.5 percentage points better than our projected probability. Unit sizes follow the Kelly criterion, scaled so the average play is about one unit.

title: NBA First Basket Picks
text:
When to bet first baskets
Early prices are often the softest, because books open before injury reports and lineups are set. Prices also jump right before tipoff when a starter is ruled out and a replacement enters the lineup. The practical approach is to take early edges when you see them and add to a play when a later alert shows a better price. More in Is There A Best Time Of Day To Bet First Baskets?

Do free throws count as a first basket?
It depends on the book. Some markets are “first basket” (any points, including free throws) and some are “first field goal” (free throws excluded). Our models project both, and each alert names the market it applies to.


Which sportsbooks offer first basket props?
In 2025-26 our alerts covered DraftKings, FanDuel, BetRivers, Hard Rock, bet365, BetMGM, Fanatics, Caesars and theScore. DraftKings and FanDuel carry the most markets and most of our volume. Prices for the same player often differ by hundreds of points between books, so the alerts list every book where the play qualifies.


Why are there so many first basket picks per game?
Because there are many markets per game: first basket, exact method, by team and by team exact, each at several books. In 2025-26 we alerted about 35 first-basket plays per game day. The unit sizes show which edges are largest, and you can filter to the markets and books you use in the Dashboard.


Do you project first basket of the second half?
Not yet. We project first-event props for the start of the game only, and only for games on the day they are played.

title: MLB NRFI & YRFI Picks
text:
Home›MLB Picks›MLB NRFI & YRFI Picks
NRFI and YRFI are bets on whether either team scores in the first inning. We project the first-inning run probability for every MLB game with the same simulation that prices our home run picks, compare it to the prices at 13 sportsbooks and exchanges twice an hour, and alert the games where a book is at least 1.5 percentage points off our number. Since launch on July 16, 2026, 553 alerted first-inning plays returned +20 net units, a 3.3% return on units staked.

title: MLB NRFI & YRFI Picks
text:
What NRFI and YRFI are

NRFI (no run first inning): neither team scores in the first inning. Wins about half the time in a typical season, so prices sit near even money.
YRFI (yes run first inning): at least one run is scored by either team in the first inning.

Both depend on the two starting pitchers, the top of each lineup, the park and the weather. A wager is usually settled by the end of the first inning, which makes these the fastest-resolving props in baseball.

title: MLB NRFI & YRFI Picks
section: How we project the first inning
text:
How we project the first inning
The simulation plays every game 20,000 times, plate appearance by plate appearance. For the first inning that means the actual projected top three or four hitters on each side against the actual starter, in that park, in that day’s forecast, with the exact plate-appearance solve described in Part 2 of our home run series. The share of simulations with a first-inning run is our YRFI probability, and NRFI is the rest. Because the same simulation produces the home run odds, the two markets are priced consistently with each other.

title: MLB Home Run Picks
text:
Home›MLB Picks›MLB Home Run Picks
We price every batter’s chance of a home run in every MLB game, then compare that price to what 13 sportsbooks and exchanges are offering, twice an hour, all day. When a book’s price is at least 2 percentage points better than our projection, it is a play. Since launch on July 16, 2026, 2,912 alerted home run plays returned +142 net units, a 5.3% return on units staked.

title: MLB Home Run Picks
section: What a home run bet is
text:
What a home run bet is
A home run prop is a wager that a batter hits at least one home run in the game, usually priced between +250 and +900. Books also offer 2+ home runs and 3+ home runs at much longer prices. A batter who does not play, or is lifted before a plate appearance in some books’ rules, has the wager voided. Home runs happen in about 3% of plate appearances, so the win rate on these plays is low and the results depend on long-run edge, not on any one night.

title: MLB Home Run Picks
text:
How we project home runs
The projection starts with the pitch. A chain of boosted-tree models, trained on about six million pitches of Statcast data, predicts what each pitcher throws to each batter, whether the batter swings, what happens on the swing, and what happens on contact, using about 145 inputs per pitch: batter and pitcher profiles, platoon splits, park dimensions in every direction, elevation, temperature and wind. For every matchup we solve the plate appearance exactly, then simulate the game 20,000 times, with lineups turning over, starters tiring, bullpens, pinch hitters and score effects. The share of simulations in which a batter homers is his probability, after a calibration step that corrects the simulator’s small biases.
Home runs are overwhelmingly a batter skill in the data. A pitcher’s home-run history carries almost no predictive weight on its own; what matters is what he throws and where the game is played. The four-part series starts with Part 1: Pitch Data; Part 3 covers edges and sizing.

title: MLB Home Run Picks
text:
Line shopping matters most here
The same batter can be +600 at one book and +900 at another on the same day, which is the difference between an implied 14.3% and 10%. On longshots, taking the best available price is worth more than almost anything else you can do. The alerts rank the books for you, and the Dashboard shows how each book’s price has moved through the day.

When do home run picks post?
The first alerts post after the 6am ET refresh, and new or improved plays post every 30 minutes until first pitch. The largest changes come when lineups are posted, usually three to five hours before the game, and when the hourly forecast shifts. Projections freeze when the game starts.


Why half-Kelly instead of full Kelly?
Full Kelly assumes the probabilities are exactly right. Ours are calibrated but not perfect, and half-Kelly cuts the size of the drawdowns when a projection is off while keeping most of the growth. Our basketball picks use a full-Kelly formula with a different normalization; the home run markets are longer-priced and more volatile.


Do the picks include Kalshi, Novig and ProphetX?
Their prices appear in the tables, and they are sometimes the best number on the board, but they are not counted as official plays. Exchange prices move fast and the resting liquidity is often too thin to guarantee the posted price is actually available. Our tracked record uses sportsbook prices only.

title: What Do NRFI and YRFI Mean? The First-Inning Bet, Explained
text:
Home›Guides›What Do NRFI and YRFI Mean? The First-Inning Bet, Explained
NRFI stands for no run first inning and YRFI for yes run first inning. It is a two-sided bet on whether either team scores in the first inning of an MLB game. The bet settles after six outs, before most people have found their seats, which is a big part of why it has become one of the most popular baseball props.

title: What Do NRFI and YRFI Mean? The First-Inning Bet, Explained
text:
How it is graded

NRFI wins if the first inning ends with the score 0-0. YRFI wins if either team scores at least one run in the top or bottom of the first.
Any run counts: earned, unearned, a wild pitch, a balk, a bases-loaded walk.
A run that scores on a play that ends the inning still counts if it crosses before the third out, following the normal scoring rules.
If the game is postponed before the first pitch, the bet is void. If a rain delay interrupts the first inning and the game resumes, the bet stands on the completed inning. If a game is suspended during the first inning and finished another day, rules vary by book; most settle on the completed inning whenever it is finished.
The market is not affected by anything that happens after the first inning, including a called game.

title: What Do NRFI and YRFI Mean? The First-Inning Bet, Explained
text:
What the odds look like
Both sides are usually priced between -105 and -135, with the favorite depending on the starters. Two aces in a pitcher’s park push NRFI toward -140; two back-end starters at Coors Field push YRFI there instead. Unlike first baskets, there is no long shot: this is an even-money market where the edge is a few percentage points, so the price you take matters as much as the side.

title: What Do NRFI and YRFI Mean? The First-Inning Bet, Explained
text:
How often NRFI hits
Roughly half of all games. In the 2026 regular season, 49.4% of MLB games had no first-inning run, and the rate by team ran from about 38% to 60%. The spread by starting pitcher is much wider: the best starters keep the first inning clean in about 90% of starts, the worst in under 50%. The MLB NRFI stats page has every team and every starter with 15 or more starts, and each team’s page has its home and away splits and month-by-month record.

title: What Do NRFI and YRFI Mean? The First-Inning Bet, Explained
text:
What moves the price

The starting pitchers, more than anything. First-inning run rates vary by starter far more than by team.
The top of each lineup. Only the first three to five hitters on each side usually bat in the first, so a lineup change at the top matters and a change at the bottom does not.
The park and the weather. Elevation, temperature and wind direction all move home run and run probability, and the first inning is played in the day’s posted conditions.
Platoon splits. A left-handed starter against a lineup stacked with right-handed hitters, or the reverse.

Our model prices every pitch from Statcast data, simulates the game 20,000 times with that day’s starters, lineups and weather, and compares the first-inning result to the posted prices. The tracked record is on the MLB NRFI and YRFI picks page, and Part 2 of the home run series explains the simulation.

What does NRFI mean in betting?
No run first inning: a bet that neither team scores in the first inning of a baseball game. YRFI, yes run first inning, is the opposite side.


What happens to an NRFI bet if the game is rained out?
If the game is postponed before it starts, the bet is void and the stake is returned. If the first inning is completed, the bet settles on it regardless of what happens to the rest of the game.


Does an unearned run count for YRFI?
Yes. Any run that crosses the plate in the first inning, however it scores, settles YRFI.


Is NRFI a good bet?
It is a good bet at a good price, and a bad bet at a bad one. Because both sides are near even money, the edge comes from pricing the specific starters, lineups and conditions better than the book. A team’s season NRFI rate is useful context but is already in the price.

title: What Is a Home Run Prop Bet? 1+ and 2+ Home Run Odds, Explained
text:
Home›Guides›What Is a Home Run Prop Bet? 1+ and 2+ Home Run Odds, Explained
A home run prop is a bet that a named batter hits at least one home run in a game. Books list it as “to hit a home run”, “1+ HR” or “anytime home run”, and it is available on every batter in every starting lineup, usually from a couple of hours after lineups post until first pitch. It is the market behind our MLB home run picks.

title: What Is a Home Run Prop Bet? 1+ and 2+ Home Run Odds, Explained
text:
The markets

1+ home run: the batter hits at least one home run. The standard market.
2+ home runs: at least two in the same game. Much longer prices, typically +1500 to +5000.
3+ home runs: rare and very long. A novelty at most books.
First home run of the game, home run in the first inning and team totals exist at some books but are thinner markets with less liquidity.

title: What Is a Home Run Prop Bet? 1+ and 2+ Home Run Odds, Explained
text:
How it is graded

The bet wins on any home run credited to the batter in the box score, including an inside-the-park home run. A home run in extra innings counts.
If the batter does not appear in the game, the bet is void and refunded at nearly every book.
If the batter is not in the starting lineup but pinch-hits or enters as a substitute, most books grade the bet on whatever happens, so it stands and usually loses. A few void it. Check the market rules the first time you bet at a book.
A game that is called early settles on the official box score if the game is official, and is void at most books if it is not.
A rained-out game is void. A suspended game that is completed later is graded on the completed game at most books.

title: What Is a Home Run Prop Bet? 1+ and 2+ Home Run Odds, Explained
text:
What the odds look like
Prices for 1+ home run run from about +200 for an elite power hitter in a hitter’s park on a windy day to +900 and beyond for a light-hitting middle infielder. The better the hitter and the better the conditions, the shorter the price. Because most batters homer in well under 20% of games, almost every price is a plus number, and almost every bettor loses most of their bets while waiting for the ones that pay.

title: What Is a Home Run Prop Bet? 1+ and 2+ Home Run Odds, Explained
section: Why line shopping matters here more than anywhere
text:
Why line shopping matters here more than anywhere
Home run prices for the same batter routinely differ by 100 to 300 points between books, and on the longer prices the difference between +600 and +800 is the difference between a bet with an edge and a bet without one. In 2026 our alerts compared 13 sportsbooks and exchanges on every batter and listed each book where a play qualified. Part 3 of the home run series shows the math.

title: What Is a Home Run Prop Bet? 1+ and 2+ Home Run Odds, Explained
text:
What drives the price

The batter: raw power, contact quality, strikeout rate, and how they fare against the day’s starter’s pitch mix.
The starting pitcher and, later in the game, the bullpen the batter is likely to face.
The park: dimensions, elevation and the published park factors by handedness.
The weather: temperature and, most of all, wind direction relative to that specific park’s orientation. Wind “blowing out” means different things at Wrigley and at Oracle Park.
Lineup spot, because the leadoff hitter gets one more plate appearance than the ninth hitter on an average night.

Our model prices each pitch from Statcast data, simulates every game 20,000 times with that day’s lineups and forecast, and alerts a play when a book’s price is at least 2 percentage points better than the projection. The record since launch is on the MLB home run picks page, and the series starts with Part 1: Pitch Data.

What does “1+ home run” mean?
The batter hits at least one home run in the game. It is the same market as “to hit a home run” or “anytime home run”.


What happens to a home run bet if the player is scratched?
If the batter does not appear in the game at all, the bet is void and the stake is refunded at nearly every sportsbook.


Does a pinch-hit home run count?
Yes, if the bet stands. At most books a bet on a player who starts on the bench stands once they enter the game, so a pinch-hit home run wins. A few books void bets on non-starters; check the rules.


What are good home run odds?
Any price longer than the batter’s real chance that day. A 15% hitter is fair at about +567, so +700 is a bet and +450 is not, and the same batter’s price differs by book. That is what our alerts check 30 times a day.

title: First Basket Exact Method, Explained: Player Plus How They Score
text:
Home›Guides›First Basket Exact Method, Explained: Player Plus How They Score
First basket exact method is the first basket market with one more condition: you pick the player and the way they score. Instead of “Jalen Brunson first basket” you bet “Jalen Brunson first basket, two-pointer” or “Jalen Brunson first basket, three-pointer”. Getting the player right but the method wrong loses. The payoff is a much longer price.

title: First Basket Exact Method, Explained: Player Plus How They Score
text:
The methods
Books split the first score into some combination of:

Two-pointer: any made field goal inside the arc, including layups, dunks, hooks and jumpers.
Three-pointer: a made shot from behind the arc.
Free throw: offered only on first-points versions of the market, where a free throw can be the first score.

Some books go further and offer the first basket type on its own (two, three or free throw, any player), and some offer the by-team exact method, the first scorer for one team with the method attached. The by-team version has two winners per game and shorter prices.

title: First Basket Exact Method, Explained: Player Plus How They Score
text:
How it is graded

The method is whatever the official play-by-play records for the qualifying score. A shot from the corner with a foot on the line is a two-pointer because that is how it was scored, not because of where the shooter meant to be.
An and-one is a made two- or three-pointer with a foul. The field goal is the first basket, graded by its method; the free throw that follows is irrelevant.
If the first points of the game are free throws, a first-field-goal exact method market is still decided by the first made field goal that follows. A first-points exact method market pays the free throw option.
If your player does not play, the bet is void at nearly every book. If they play and someone else scores first, or they score first by the other method, it loses.

title: First Basket Exact Method, Explained: Player Plus How They Score
text:
What the odds look like
Prices start around +600 for a center’s two-pointer and run past +5000 for a guard’s three-pointer or a reserve’s anything. The longest prices are where our biggest single wins have come from: a +8000 two-pointer by Dean Wade on New Year’s Day 2024 returned 97 units on a 1.2-unit stake. The 2023-24 biggest hits post lists ten like it.
Because the prices are so long, the market loses far more often than it wins. In the 2025-26 NBA season, Slam Dunk Bets won 90 of 1,239 exact-method wagers, about 7%, and the market still returned a 40% profit on units staked, because the prices on the winners were longer than their real chance. The full record is on the NBA first basket picks page.

title: First Basket Exact Method, Explained: Player Plus How They Score
text:
Why the market is beatable
Exact method asks the book to price two things at once: who shoots first and what kind of shot it is. Books get the method part wrong more often than the player part. A big man’s two-pointer is usually priced well, but a forward who often takes a catch-and-shoot three on the first possession, or a center who gets the opening lob, can be priced far below their real rate. Our models predict the method separately from the player and combine them; Part 3 of the first basket series explains the modeling, and the team stats pages show how each team’s first baskets were actually scored.

title: First Basket Exact Method, Explained: Player Plus How They Score
text:
Managing the variance
Long odds mean long losing streaks, with wins arriving in bunches. The sensible approach is small, consistent stakes sized to the edge, which is what our unit sizes do: a 0.5-unit alert on a +4000 price is normal, and a 3-unit alert is rare. See what is a unit for how the sizes are set, and do not judge the market on a month.

What does “first basket exact method” mean?
A bet on which player scores the game’s first basket and how they score it: a two-pointer, a three-pointer, or at some books a free throw. Both parts have to be right.


How is an and-one graded in an exact method market?
As the field goal that was made. A layup plus a foul is a two-pointer; the free throw afterward does not change the result.


What are typical first basket exact method odds?
Roughly +600 to +1500 for a likely first scorer’s most likely method, and +2000 to +10000 for everything else. Prices for the same player and method can differ by thousands of points between books.


Is exact method a good bet?
Only at the right price. It wins rarely, so it needs an edge that the model can quantify, small stakes, and a long enough sample to let the math work. Our record in the market, season by season, is on the NBA first basket picks page.

title: What Is a First Basket Bet? How It Works and How It’s Graded
text:
Home›Guides›What Is a First Basket Bet? How It Works and How It’s Graded
A first basket bet is a wager on which player scores first in a basketball game. It settles within the first minute or two, it is offered on every NBA and WNBA game at most sportsbooks, and the odds on a starter usually run from about +300 for the favorite to +1500 and beyond for the rest of the lineup. It is also the market Slam Dunk Bets was built on, so this page covers the rules in more detail than most.

title: What Is a First Basket Bet? How It Works and How It’s Graded
section: First basket, first field goal, first points
text:
First basket, first field goal, first points
Books use “first basket” loosely, and the fine print matters:

First field goal: the first made field goal of the game. Free throws do not count. This is the most common version.
First points: the first points of any kind. A player who is fouled on the opening possession and makes a free throw wins this market but not the field-goal version.
First basket: whichever of the two the book has decided it means. Check the market rules; the same book can use different rules in different states.

The difference comes up more than you would think. In the 2025-26 NBA season, the game’s first points and its first field goal went to different players in about 8% of games. The NBA first basket stats page tracks that number every season.

title: What Is a First Basket Bet? How It Works and How It’s Graded
text:
The variants

First basket by team: the first player to score for one specific team, regardless of who scores first in the game. Two winners per game, so prices are shorter.
First basket exact method: the player and how they score, for example a three-pointer or a dunk. Much longer odds. See the exact method guide.
First basket type: how the game’s first points are scored (two, three, free throw), regardless of player.
Team to score first: which team scores first, often paired with a win-tipoff market. Covered on the NBA team to score first page.
First basket of the second half: offered by some books; we do not project it yet.

title: What Is a First Basket Bet? How It Works and How It’s Graded
text:
How it is graded

The winner is the player credited with the qualifying score in the official play-by-play. A tip-in or a goaltended shot counts for the player credited with the points.
If your player does not play at all, nearly every book voids the bet and refunds the stake. If the player plays but does not score first, the bet loses. Whether a player who is listed as a starter but ruled out at tipoff is void depends on the book; most void.
An “and-one” (a made basket with a foul) counts as a field goal at the moment the shot goes in, so the shooter wins the field-goal market before the free throw is attempted.
Each-way and “no player” options exist at some books. Read the market rules the first time you bet at a new one.

title: What Is a First Basket Bet? How It Works and How It’s Graded
text:
What the odds look like
The favorite is usually the team’s primary scorer or its center, because the first possession of most games is a set play run for one of them. In 2025-26 the median price Slam Dunk Bets bet in these markets was +600, which a book prices as roughly a 14% chance. Even the best first-basket player in the league scores first for their team in about 40% of starts; see the leaders table on the stats page.
Prices move all day. Books open the market before injury reports and starting lineups are confirmed, and the biggest moves come in the hour before tipoff when a starter is ruled out and a replacement enters the lineup. Our timing article covers how to handle that.

title: What Is a First Basket Bet? How It Works and How It’s Graded
section: Why first baskets can be beaten
text:
Why first baskets can be beaten
Books price this market inconsistently and popular players are usually overpriced because they attract the most action. Role players who take the first shot in a set play, or who move into the starting lineup when someone sits, are often priced below their real chance. That mispricing is the reason we started modeling first baskets in 2020, and the tracked results are on the NBA first basket picks and WNBA first basket picks pages.

Do free throws count as a first basket?
Only in a first-points market. A first-field-goal market ignores free throws, and most books that say “first basket” mean first field goal. The market rules at your book settle it.


What happens if my first basket player doesn’t start?
If the player does not play at all, the bet is voided and refunded at nearly every book. If the player comes off the bench, the bet stands and almost always loses, because the first basket is scored long before a reserve enters.


What are typical first basket odds?
About +300 to +500 for a team’s most likely first scorer, +600 to +1200 for the rest of the starting lineup, and longer for reserves. Odds for the same player regularly differ by hundreds of points between books, which is why our alerts list every book where a play qualifies.


Who scores the first basket most often?
It changes every season, and it is as much about who takes the first shot as who makes it. The NBA leaders and WNBA leaders pages list the top players and every team’s most frequent first scorer.

title: What Is a Unit in Sports Betting? Units, Net Units and ROI, Explained
text:
Home›Guides›What Is a Unit in Sports Betting? Units, Net Units and ROI, Explained
A unit is a bettor’s standard bet size. Instead of saying “I won $340 last month”, a bettor says “I’m up 3.4 units”, and everyone who hears it can translate it into their own money. Units make a record comparable across bettors with different bankrolls and let a picks service publish results without telling you how much to risk.

title: What Is a Unit in Sports Betting? Units, Net Units and ROI, Explained
text:
What a unit is worth
Whatever you decide. The usual advice is 1% to 2% of your bankroll, so a bettor with $5,000 set aside for betting has a $50 to $100 unit. Common units are $100, $10 and $1. The point is that it stays fixed: a 2-unit bet is always twice a 1-unit bet, whatever the dollar amount.

title: What Is a Unit in Sports Betting? Units, Net Units and ROI, Explained
text:
Net units and ROI
Two numbers describe a record:

Net units is profit measured in units: everything won minus everything lost. A +600 bet of 1 unit that wins is +6 units; one that loses is -1.
ROI (return on investment) is net units divided by units staked. Win 160 units on 1,000 staked and the ROI is 16%.

Both matter. A big net-unit number on a huge volume of bets can hide a thin margin, and a high ROI on a tiny sample means nothing yet. Our season recaps show both, with the number of wagers next to them: in the 2025-26 NBA season, 16,949 wagers returned +2,135 net units on 13,059 units staked, a 16.3% ROI. The 2025-26 recap breaks it down.

title: What Is a Unit in Sports Betting? Units, Net Units and ROI, Explained
section: What a realistic ROI looks like
text:
What a realistic ROI looks like
On sides and totals, a long-run ROI of 3% to 5% is excellent, because the books’ margin is small and the markets are efficient. Prop markets like first baskets and home runs are priced less carefully, so the achievable margin is wider, and the variance is far higher: a 16% ROI on first baskets arrives with weeks of losses between the wins. Any record should be judged on thousands of bets, not dozens, and the FAQ lists ours season by season.

title: What Is a Unit in Sports Betting? Units, Net Units and ROI, Explained
section: How our unit sizes are set
text:
How our unit sizes are set
Every play Slam Dunk Bets alerts carries a recommended size, such as 1.4u. The sizes come from the Kelly criterion, a formula that stakes more when the edge is larger and the odds shorter, and less on long prices. We scale the result so that the average play is about one unit, which means:

A 3-unit recommendation marks one of the largest edges of the day.
A 0.3-unit recommendation on a +5000 price is normal; long shots get small stakes on purpose.
For MLB we use half-Kelly, a more conservative version, because baseball margins are thinner.

You do not have to bet every play, and you should not bet the units literally if they add up to more than you are comfortable with on a busy night. Treat the sizes as a ranking of edges and scale them to your own unit. Part 4 of the first basket series explains the sizing, and the Slam Dunk Dashboard includes a unit-sizing calculator.

title: What Is a Unit in Sports Betting? Units, Net Units and ROI, Explained
text:
Standardized units in our records
Our published records use standardized units, with wager sizes normalized so the average recommended bet is about one unit, and ROI measured on units actually staked, with voided bets excluded. The first tracked season, 2021-22, was bet at flat stakes before Kelly sizing was introduced. All of this is spelled out in the FAQ and in each season recap’s “How we counted” section.

What is a unit in betting?
A bettor’s standard stake, chosen once and kept fixed, usually 1% to 2% of the bankroll. Results are then reported in units so they can be compared without dollar amounts.


How much money is one unit?
Whatever you set it to. $100, $10 and $1 are common. A record of +2,135 units means +$21,350 at a $10 unit and +$2,135 at a $1 unit.


What is a good ROI in sports betting?
A few percent on sides and totals over the long run. Prop markets allow more, with more variance; our NBA seasons have ranged from 8% to 17% on tens of thousands of wagers.


Why do your alerts recommend different unit sizes?
Because the edges differ. A Kelly-based formula stakes more on larger edges and shorter prices and less on long shots, scaled so the average play is about one unit.

title: MLB Prop Picks: Home Runs, NRFI & YRFI
text:
How the picks work
Statcast publishes about 119 columns on every pitch. We mirror all of it back to 2017 and build batter, pitcher, park and weather profiles on top. A chain of boosted-tree models predicts each pitch: what is thrown, whether the batter swings, what happens on the swing and what happens on contact. For every matchup we solve the plate appearance exactly, then simulate the game 20,000 times with lineups, bullpens, pinch hitters and score effects. A calibration layer trues the output up so that a published 12% means 12%. The four-part series starts with Part 1: Pitch Data.
A home run play is alerted when a book’s price is at least 2 percentage points better than our projection (1.5 points for multi-homer and first-inning markets). Unit sizes are half-Kelly, scaled so the average play is about one unit.

Models retrain every Monday. Every morning at 6am ET there is a full refresh, then a tick every 30 minutes from 7am to 10pm ET: new pitch data, posted lineups and probable starters, an hourly forecast for every park, and a re-simulation of every game whose inputs changed. Does weather really matter for home run picks?
Yes. Every forecast is resolved against the compass bearing from home plate to center field in that park, so “wind blowing out” means blowing out in that stadium specifically. Temperature, elevation and roof status are inputs too. Domes are modeled as 72°F and windless.

title: 2023-24 NBA ROI Recap: Biggest Hits
text:
The top 10 single-bet wins

Dean Wade, first player to score exact method 2-pointer, Jan 1 2024

+8000 odds at MGM, 1.2u wager, 97u return
HAPPY NEW YEAR! Wade rarely took the first shot, and tended toward 3-pointers, so MGM gave us that big line.

Vince Williams Jr., first player to score exact method 2-pointer, Jan 13 2024

+5000 odds at MGM, 1.5u wager, 74u return
Vince showed up 43 times in our plays, almost always at MGM, and hit 6 of them

Noah Clowney, first player to score exact method 2-pointer, Apr 12 2024

+2200 at Draftkings, 3u wager, 65u ROI
This shot shows up twice - the beauty of correlated markets!

Scottie Barnes, first player to score exact method 3-pointer, Dec 23 2023

+7000 at Fanduel, 0.9u wager, 65u ROI
Who says big men can’t hit from long range? This moved closer to +4000 by end of season.

Noah Clowney, first player to score by team exact method 2-pointer, Apr 12 2024

+1300 at Draftkings, 4.5u wager, 59u ROI
The second hit from this same shot, both times at DK

Trayce Jackson-Davis, first player to score by team exact method 2-pointer, Jan 2 2024

+470 at Caesars, 10.5u wager, 49u ROI
Our biggest individual wager of the year at 10.5 units, netted 49 for the courageous

Markelle Fultz, first 3-pointer by team, Feb 6 2024

+4000 at Draftkings, 1.1u wager, 46u ROI
Fultz was overall a 10.3 unit return, so it was basically this and then nothing else

Terance Mann, first player to score exact method 3-pointer, Jan 10 2024

+5000 at MGM, .9u wager, 45u ROI
We got value on TM frequently on first 3-pointer plays as well

Nikola Jovic, first 3-pointer, Feb 13 2024

+1600 at Draftkings, 2.8u wager, 44u ROI
this was one of our first hits on the first 3-pointer market

Trayce Jackson-Davis, first basket by team, Jan 2 2024

+500 at Fanduel, 8.1u wager, 40.5u ROI
our second biggest wager of the year (yeah January 2nd was a big day of betting) and the second leg of a massive ROI on TJD for the day

title: 2023-24 NBA ROI Recap: Biggest Hits
section: What the list has in common
text:
What the list has in common
Eight of the ten came from exact-method markets, where a book has to price not just who scores first but how. That’s where our exact-method models earn their keep, and it’s why the unit sizes are small: these are longshots, sized by Kelly, and most of them lose. The ones that hit pay for a lot of the ones that don’t.
Thanks as always for reading, and please consider subscribing if you haven’t yet!

title: 2023-24 NBA ROI Recap: Top 5 ROI Players
text: In prep for the 2024-25 NBA season we’re looking back at some of the highlights from the 2023-24 season (where we were up 1692 units).

title: 2023-24 NBA ROI Recap: Top 5 ROI Players
section: The top five by net units
text:
The top five by net units
Here were the top 5 players from 2023-24, from a net ROI perspective. We’re showing how many bets we made on that player over the year (across all first basket type markets), how many wins we hit, our net ROI in units, as well as an ROI %.

Scoot Henderson, Portland Trailblazers

102 bets, 30 wins, net 150 units, 109% ROI
He didn’t always start at PG, but when he did, he was heavily involved early in the game; he wasn’t efficient but could follow up a missed jumper with a tip.

Bradley Beal, Phoenix Suns

149 bets, 39 wins, net 122 units, 103% ROI
Our 6th most heavily wagered, Beal was bound to be a consistent value in lineups with KD, Booker, and Nurk drawing a lot of the action.

Josh Giddey, Oklahoma City Thunder

167 bets, 42 wins, net 118 units, 71% ROI
Like Beal but less efficient from an ROI perspective, we bet on Giddey to score first for the Thunder basically every game they played, more than all but 3 other players all season, while the rest of the world bet on SGA and Chet (not saying we liked it!).

Andrew Wiggins, Golden State Warriors

92 bets, 31 wins, net 84 units, 112% ROI
Another part-time starter who benefited from odds depressed due to playing with superstar shooters, i.e. Steph Curry and Klay Thompson.

Ivica Zubac, Los Angeles Clippers

107 bets, 23 wins, net 73 units, 59% ROI
We bet on Zoobs a lot, especially on first basket exact methods two-pointer plays and first basket by team; like most other players on this list, which is why his ROI is markedly lower than others so far.

title: 2023-24 NBA ROI Recap: Top 5 ROI Players
text:
Why these players kept paying
The common thread is usage the books underrated: part-time starters, and secondary scorers playing next to stars who soaked up the betting action. That’s the same pattern we described in Why First Baskets?, and it’s exactly what our player to score first models are built to find.
Most of those players netted us more by themselves than other services are netting in total. Fun fact though - none of the players in this list are represented in any of the top 10 single biggest wins from 2023-24. We check those out in the biggest hits recap.
Thanks as always for reading, and please consider subscribing if you haven’t yet!

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 2: The Data We Use
text: First two posts in this series were very high level, now we get into some specifics. What data are we using to predict first basket outcomes?

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 2: The Data We Use
section: Play-by-play and box scores from the league
text:
Play-by-play and box scores from the league
The vast majority of the information we need comes directly from the NBA’s play-by-play and boxscore records. Here’s an example of what the NBA generates and freely shares for every game. Outside of the play-by-play data, we can also grab some basic player information (height, weight, age, draft position) from the NBA’s player information portal.

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 2: The Data We Use
section: Starting lineups and sportsbook game lines
text:
Starting lineups and sportsbook game lines
There are a couple of important data elements we use that we get from outside the NBA’s records. The first is starting lineup information - it turns out, everybody and their cousin has a twitter account or website with the projected starting lineups for every game, so we use one of them (for free) for lineup info.
The second is game lines from sportsbooks. The spread, total, and moneyline for NBA games typically have a lot of information in them, because it is influenced by 1) bookmakers, who have models and good info in most cases and 2) bettors, who can move the betting lines by making more and bigger wagers on one side than another. We track game lines from several sportsbooks.

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 2: The Data We Use
text:
How we collect it
To be clear, we’re not manually downloading a bunch of pdf’s or clicking into sportsbook apps and recording the odds in a spreadsheet. We use data science tools to programmatically access data from APIs (there are dozens of them! try the nba_api python library if that’s your jam), and add them to our data store. Most of the data we care about only update once a day, like play-by-play records from the previous day, but some of it is updated as often as every 30 minutes, like starting lineup information, and sportsbook lines.

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 2: The Data We Use
text:
Cleaning, labeling and feature engineering
Once we get the data, we have to do a bunch of additional work, including: validating that the data are sensible and not buggy or duplicated or other things that happen to data; label when jump balls and first baskets (and first other things) happen, and who does them, and the specific method it happened; engineer common and bespoke metrics, like efficiency, and first-basket-related usage rates, conditioned on specific lineups; aggregate statistics within games, and seasons, and players, and teams, and coaches, and different combinations of those levels, using lots of different operations; create rolling window functions so we can calculate metrics in specific windows of time or stretches of games; and then lots of recoding and normalizing to get things prepped for our modeling pipelines.
Whew! It sounds like a lot when its all written out like this, but most of our data pipelines run in way less than an hour.

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 2: The Data We Use
section: What we’d still like to add
text:
What we’d still like to add
Like most curious folks, we’re always on the lookout for additional data that can help our models perform better. I suspect that we’re getting as much information as we can out of the play-by-play data; we might benefit from adding additional coach-specific information into the models, if we think that there are coach-related patterns that might explain some variance in first basket/early game usage and success; or similar to coaching-related variance, there’s possibly some aspect of how a team is doing with respect to making the playoffs that could explain some variance as well.
The ultimate criteria for whether we use data in our models is, “does it make the model better?” Which at this point is a high bar to cross 😎
Next up is a deeper dive into the models themselves in Part 3 (not like a SUPER deep dive, but more than what was in the last post on this). Thanks for reading, and thanks even more if you subscribe!

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 4: From Predictions To Edges
text:
Being able to estimate odds for first baskets is a nifty parlor trick that might give you something to talk about at a job interview or the bar or whatever, but unless we can find opportunities where our predictions can give us a betting edge, they’re not especially useful.
Fortunately, we can - and do - find edges aplenty! Here’s how.

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 4: From Predictions To Edges
section: Getting semi-realtime odds from the books
text:
Getting semi-realtime odds from the books
First, and we’re sure this goes entirely without saying, we don’t EVER violate or advocate that others violate the terms and conditions of service of sportsbook apps or websites. That’d be morally wrong, and would put us at risk of having our accounts limited even further or shut down entirely (or worse!). You should never break those, or any rules. Ever. Got it? Good.
That out of the way, we built some tools to get semi-realtime odds from the most popular books available in North America. This is a pain in the ass, because sportsbooks don’t want people to be able to shop around easily, and instead of putting in modernized safeguards against bad actors, the books just use the jankiest sets of data models and practices that you might expect out of a dorm room startup, which is like a “security by stupidity” strategy. We have opinions here, but we digress.
Once we get the odds, we have to reconcile them with our data. Books are intentionally inconsistent with how they list player and team names, and you’d be shocked at how often they misspell things or list players on the wrong teams, so we have to do some lightweight NLP to map everything together.

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 4: From Predictions To Edges
text:
What counts as an edge
After that, we built tools that identify cases where a book is offering odds that are at least 1% longer than what our model predicts. To explain: odds can be translated to probabilities; we compare the probabilities from our model to the odds offered by the books; if our model predicts a player has a 10% chance to score first in the game (translates exactly to +900), but a book offers that player at odds equivalent to 11.11% (+800), we see that 11.11% - 10% = 1.11% which is greater than our threshold.
Update 2024-12-10: We now use a 1.5% threshold for determining a playable edge!
We usually observe 1-6 edges per game at or beyond our threshold for first basket plays in both the NBA and WNBA. And that’s just for the first basket overall market - when you factor in the first basket by team and exact methods plays, we’re seeing between one and two dozen plays per game just on first basket markets.
I know right? Bananas.

title: How Do You Predict First Baskets? Part 4: From Predictions To Edges
section: Unit sizing with the Kelly criterion
text:
Unit sizing with the Kelly criterion
Edited to Add: Dang I forgot about the recommended unit size calculations when I first published this. Our unit recommendations are just Kelly Criterion with a twist! We use Fully Kelly, but then we adjust based on the average unit size recommendation within a prop market, so that the average recommended bet within each market is 1 unit. This makes it a lot easier to calibrate your outlay based on a market’s ROI, e.g. you can use a bigger unit for more profitable markets. (I bet people will have opinions about this.)
Anyways, the next part of this, Part 5, will be about the alerts themselves, which involves some conversation about AI! Check it out, and also subscribe if you haven’t yet, it helps us make tools and content 🙏
